summary: An experimental document that specifies ICMP messages for reporting failures when using the IP security protocols AH and ESP, such as when a packet fails authentication or decryption.

plainLanguage.summary: When a secret message is rejected, the receiver can send back a short note explaining the problem. This document defines those notes.

subtitle: ICMP messages for reporting authentication, encryption, and authorization failures in IPsec

tldr.problem: When IP Security Protocol (IPsec) headers are processed and an error occurs—such as a bad Security Parameters Index, failed authentication, or lack of authorization—there is no standard way to report this error back to the sender.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines ICMP Type 40 messages with six different codes for different IPsec failures: Bad SPI, Authentication Failed, Decompression Failed, Decryption Failed, Need Authentication, and Need Authorization.
tldr.outcome: When IPsec processing fails, the receiver can send a standardized error message that includes the original IP headers and part of the payload, allowing the sender to match the error to the original packet and determine the next action.

facts.label: Payload included
facts.value: Original IP headers + first 64 bits of payload

today: RFC 2521 remains Experimental. It was proposed as a way for systems using IPsec to report security-related failures, but it has not been widely deployed. Modern IPsec implementations (such as those using IKEv2 key management) handle failures through the key management protocol rather than through these ICMP messages.

sections.title: Reporting IPsec Errors
sections.content:
The Internet Protocol Security architecture defines how to apply encryption and authentication to IP traffic. When a system receives an IPsec-protected packet, it must verify authentication, decrypt if needed, and check if the sender is authorized. If any of these steps fail, the receiver needs a way to report the problem.

This document specifies ICMP messages for this purpose. These messages are useful for both statically configured security associations (where an operator needs to manually fix the configuration) and for automated key management protocols that detect failures and attempt to renegotiate.
sections.plainLanguage: When a protected message fails checks, the receiver sends back an ICMP error message saying what went wrong so the sender can fix it.

sections.title: The Message Structure
sections.content:
All these messages use ICMP Type 40. The message includes a checksum, a reserved field (for future use), and a Pointer field that indicates the byte offset in the original headers where the problematic Security Parameters Index (SPI) is located. Zero is used when no SPI is present.

The message also includes the original IP header and any intermediate headers up to the SPI, plus the first 64 bits (8 octets) of the payload data. This is enough information for the receiving host to match the error to the original packet (most protocols with port numbers put those ports in the first 64 bits).
sections.plainLanguage: The error message is a short note that copies the original message headers and the first part of the data so you can tell which packet failed.

sections.title: Six Types of Failures
sections.content:
Bad SPI (code 0): The Security Parameters Index in the packet is invalid or has expired. Authentication Failed (code 1): The packet failed the authenticity or integrity check for a given SPI; the SPI may be an outer ESP header hiding an inner Authentication Header. Decompression Failed (code 2): The packet failed a decompression check for its SPI, which can happen when IPsec includes compression.

Decryption Failed (code 3): The packet failed a decryption check for its SPI, meaning the encrypted data could not be properly decrypted. Need Authentication (code 4): The receiver will not accept the packet without additional authentication, either because no SPI is present or because an unsuitable SPI is present (for example, encryption without integrity). Need Authorization (code 5): The packet includes an authentication SPI that is inappropriate for the target transport or application; the party denoted by the SPI does not have proper authorization.
sections.plainLanguage: The error code says which check failed: bad SPI, authentication failed, decompression failed, decryption failed, need more authentication, or need authorization.

sections.title: Handling and Rate Limiting
sections.content:
Upon receipt of an uninterpretable security failure message or one that contains an error, no ICMP error message is sent in response—it is silently discarded. However, nodes SHOULD log the error for diagnosis and maintain statistics counters.

Systems MUST take special care to verify that the ICMP message actually corresponds to a previously sent IP datagram, preventing denial-of-service attacks where an attacker floods targets with bogus error messages. Implementations MUST support rate limiting of these messages; limits may be applied per destination, per interface, or by some other method. For authenticated responses (when a prior Security Association exists), these messages SHOULD be sent with authentication. However, implementations MUST NOT dynamically establish a new Security Association solely to authenticate these messages, as that would be computationally expensive and vulnerable to denial-of-service attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Broken or forged error messages are ignored silently. Valid senders should check that errors match something they sent. Messages are rate-limited to prevent flooding attacks.
